title: Spatial Dashboard Builder: Maps That Summarise
description: Assemble a simple spatial dashboard from map layers and summary panels with the Spatial Dashboard Builder — share the picture, honestly sourced. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a city team can pair one map of service locations with counts by district — a dashboard whose every panel traces back to the same open data the map shows.
quick_answer: The Spatial Dashboard Builder assembles a simple spatial dashboard — a map view accompanied by the summary panels, counts and breakdowns that make the map legible. Choose your area and layers and read the combined picture: geography plus its headline numbers, built from stated data rather than decoration.
steps_intro: A map alone is a picture; a dashboard is a picture with its evidence attached:

body.t: Facilities, coverage and counts by area in one shareable view — the format public meetings actually absorb. The underlying point patterns can be pre-mapped with the
Territories, depots and demand on one screen for the Monday meeting — a dashboard that updates its story when the data does.
The map-plus-numbers page is the modern data story. Panels force the author to state totals the map alone could insinuate.
Students who must summarise their own map stop trusting pretty choropleths blindly — building the dashboard is the lesson.

examples.label: Example · The panel disciplines the map

body.t: A heat blob looks alarming until its panel says '14 incidents, city of 900,000'. Dashboards that show counts beside colours are how spatial honesty is enforced in practice.
Counts per district versus rates per 10,000 residents tell different stories about the same points. A good dashboard states which it shows — and the population tools here supply the denominators.

Honest interactivity — what is excluded, stated
Dataset, provider and date — the dashboard's conscience
popular_table.note: This builder assembles views from open map data; it is a presentation layer, not a statistics authority. The base FAQ's 'official statistics?' question is answered by the source line you ship with it.

faq: Point and area data from the open sources MapBench works with, organised by the areas and categories you choose. The dashboard's ceiling is its data's quality — stated on the panel, always.
They reflect the data at build and refresh time. 'Live' is a claim about a feed, not a layout — where no feed exists, the dashboard shows its data's date.
Can I embed the dashboard elsewhere?
Sharing follows the creation tools' pattern — links and embeds where supported, with source licences travelling with the output.
Rates or counts — which should I show?
Rates for comparing areas of different sizes; counts for operational totals. Showing counts alone across unequal areas is the classic dashboard sin this page warns about.
No — the builder is form-driven. The trade for that ease is a fixed, honest set of panel types rather than a BI platform's infinity.
Do not put sensitive datasets into shareable public views. Aggregate first (cells and districts exist for this), then build.
Dashboards summarise; raw thousands belong in the dataset, with the dashboard as its window. Aggregate until the map reads at a glance.
